Observed facts: 65‑year‑old man with ulcerative colitis on mesalamine; five‑week febrile illness with night sweats, arthralgia, abdominal symptoms; prior admission showed inflammatory and liver‑test abnormalities, colonoscopy negative for active colitis; antibiotics and brief prednisone failed; low‑level EBV DNA, positive VCA IgM/IgG interpreted as primary EBV. New findings: palpable purpura on flanks, thighs, lower legs; transient scrotal pain; joint pain; leg oedema; urine 2+ protein, 1+ blood, 5‑10 RBC/HPF, protein:creatinine 0.99; creatinine 0.72 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL, platelets 505 000/µL; CT shows small‑bowel thickening, inflammatory change, small ascites; febrile, hemodynamically stable. Travel: West Africa, SE Asia >10 years ago; Florida 7 months ago; chicken‑coop exposure. Rapid P. falciparum antigen positive; thick/thin smears negative on two days.

Hypotheses: 1) EBV‑associated systemic illness with secondary vasculitis/renal involvement; 2) Acute malaria (false‑positive antigen or low‑level parasitaemia below smear detection) causing fever, thrombocytosis, bowel edema; 3) Henoch‑Schönlein purpura/IgA vasculitis triggered by infection (EBV or malaria) producing purpura, arthralgia, renal findings, bowel wall thickening.

Proposed actions: Repeat quantitative malaria PCR and thick smear daily for 3 days; obtain EBV quantitative PCR trend and heterophile test; urine microscopy for dysmorphic RBCs, urine protein electrophoresis; serum IgA, complement C3/C4, cryoglobulins; skin biopsy of purpura for IgA deposition; consider renal biopsy if proteinuria persists; monitor renal function, platelet trend, abdominal imaging for evolving bowel disease.

It reconciles the positive antigen with negative smears and re-evaluates the earlier EBV label rather than accepting it uncritically, and it proposes discriminating tests (skin biopsy for IgA deposition, complement, quantitative EBV PCR, repeat smears/PCR) plus renal and urinary monitoring.
